report.source_text: On examination in the neurosurgical clinic, the patient had hyperaesthesia from the neck down, most prominent in the hands and groins. The patient had reduced grip strength of 3/5, finger extension and abduction of 3/5, wrist flexion and extension of 3/5, elbow flexion of 4+/5, elbow extension of 4/5 and shoulder abduction of 4+/5 on the Medical Research Council power scale. Hip flexion was 3/5, with all other muscle groups in the lower limb at 4+/5. The patient had very brisk reflexes with pathological spreading in the upper and lower limbs. There was self-limiting clonus in the ankle bilaterally. Hoffmann’s and Babinski reflexes were positive bilaterally. There was a severe loss of coordination and balance. Gait was impaired; the patient required a frame to mobilise.

report.source_text: In addition, at 9 months the patient had an improved mJOA of 10 (3+3+2+2) and she reported improved manual dexterity, improved walking, improved bladder function and resolution of incontinence. The dysaesthesia affecting her body was still present, although reduced.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 62-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of progressive neurological symptoms including dysaesthetic sensory symptoms, falls, severely compromised walking, urinary and faecal incontinence, and reduced manual dexterity. Neurological examination revealed hyperaesthesia, significant motor weakness in upper and lower limbs, hyperreflexia with pathological signs (Hoffmann's, Babinski, clonus), and severe loss of coordination and balance (E003). MRI of the cervical spine confirmed severe multilevel degenerative changes, specifically a broad-based disc osteophyte protrusion at C3/4 causing spinal cord compression with T2 hyperintense signal changes, consistent with severe cervical myelopathy (E004). The patient underwent anterior cervical discectomy at C3/4 (E005). Post-operatively, at 3 months, she showed good recovery with reduced sensory problems and improved motor strength (E006). At 9 months, her mJOA score improved to 10, with reported improvements in manual dexterity, walking, and resolution of incontinence, although dysaesthesia persisted but was reduced (E007).

MRI of the cervical spine revealed multilevel degenerative changes with spinal cord compression and T2 hyperintense signal changes at C3/4, confirming severe cervical myelopathy.
The patient underwent anterior cervical discectomy at C3/4 for decompression.
Clinical improvement was observed post-surgery, including reduced sensory problems, improved motor strength, and resolution of incontinence.
